Plerophoria
play-ro-fo-REE-ah
n. (Greek)
Greek plērophoria, “full assurance, full conviction,” from plēro- (full) + phor- (to bear). The literal sense is “full-bearing” or “full-carrying”: the soul borne fully into conviction.

📖 Biblical Definition

Plērophoria is the New Testament’s rich word for full assurance—the settled, undoubting, soul-borne conviction of the truth of the gospel, the love of God in Christ, the hope of glory, and the believer’s own standing in the salvation announced. The word is rare in the New Testament (four uses) but each is theologically weighty. Colossians 2:2: Paul labors for the saints that their hearts might be comforted, being knit together in love, and unto all riches of the full assurance of understanding, to the acknowledgement of the mystery of God, and of the Father, and of Christ. Hebrews 6:11: and we desire that every one of you do shew the same diligence to the full assurance of hope unto the end. Hebrews 10:22: let us draw near with a true heart in full assurance of faith, having our hearts sprinkled from an evil conscience, and our bodies washed with pure water. 1 Thessalonians 1:5: for our gospel came not unto you in word only, but also in power, and in the Holy Ghost, and in much assurance. The four uses cluster into a structural doctrine. The saints are to have full assurance of understanding: the settled comprehension of God’s mystery in Christ. They are to have full assurance of hope: the settled expectation of the inheritance reserved in heaven. They are to have full assurance of faith: the settled confidence of access to the throne of grace by the blood of Jesus. And the gospel itself comes with much assurance when the Spirit accompanies the Word. Plērophoria is therefore not presumption—not the soul claiming what God has not given—but the Spirit-wrought settled persuasion of what God has in fact given: the full conviction of mind, heart, and will, that what the gospel announces is true and that the believer is included in it. The doctrine is pastorally crucial. Where assurance is absent, the saint is restless, fearful, unable to draw near with full confidence; where assurance is present, the saint can stand at the throne, walk in his calling, suffer in his trial, and die in his Lord with the settled inward certainty that what has been announced is true and that he is in it. The Reformed tradition has emphasized that plērophoria is the privilege of every believer (against traditions that have made assurance a privileged second blessing reserved for the few), is grounded in the objective work of Christ rather than the believer’s introspection (against the despair of self-examination divorced from the gospel), and is ordinarily produced by the Spirit’s witness to the Word that announces Christ. The recovery of plērophoria is therefore the recovery of the saint’s rest in what God has done.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines FULL ASSURANCE (a phrase rendering the Greek plērophoria) as entire, settled certainty of mind; the Spirit-wrought conviction of the truth of the gospel and of the believer’s standing in it; in scripture, the privilege of every believer through the Spirit’s witness to the Word.

ASSURANCE, n. — The act of assuring, or making certain or sure to one’s self; certainty. In divinity, the firm persuasion of one’s reconciliation to God, and of his salvation by faith in Christ; full and certain confidence. Let us draw near with a true heart in full assurance of faith (Heb 10:22).

PLEROPHORIA — (Greek noun, G4136.) Full assurance, full conviction. Four NT uses: Col 2:2; 1 Thess 1:5; Heb 6:11; 10:22. Etymologically full-bearing: the soul borne fully into settled conviction.

📖 Key Scripture

Colossians 2:2 — "That their hearts might be comforted, being knit together in love, and unto all riches of the full assurance of understanding, to the acknowledgement of the mystery of God, and of the Father, and of Christ."

Hebrews 6:11 — "And we desire that every one of you do shew the same diligence to the full assurance of hope unto the end."

Hebrews 10:22 — "Let us draw near with a true heart in full assurance of faith, having our hearts sprinkled from an evil conscience, and our bodies washed with pure water."

1 Thessalonians 1:5 — "For our gospel came not unto you in word only, but also in power, and in the Holy Ghost, and in much assurance; as ye know what manner of men we were among you for your sake."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Plērophoria is corrupted, on one side, by the presumption that claims assurance as a possession independent of any examination, divorcing it from the marks of regenerate life Scripture supplies—and on the other by the despair that withholds assurance as a privileged possession of the few, against the apostolic pattern that addresses ordinary saints with full-assurance language as the normal Christian standing.

expand to see more

Presumption is one corruption of plērophoria: the claim of assurance as a possession independent of any examination, divorced from the marks of regenerate life Scripture supplies. The believer who has prayed a sinner’s prayer at some past moment, who has placed himself in the category of Christian, and who therefore presumes upon assurance without any present marks of regenerate life—repentance, faith working through love, growth in holiness, the inward witness of the Spirit—has converted the biblical doctrine into a self-flattering presumption Scripture does not support. The Bible holds assurance and self-examination together: examine yourselves, whether ye be in the faith; prove your own selves. Know ye not your own selves, how that Jesus Christ is in you, except ye be reprobates? (2 Cor 13:5). The recovery is the holding together: the gospel-grounded assurance that the work of Christ is sufficient for sinners, paired with the careful self-examination that confirms the marks of regenerate life are present in fact.

The opposite corruption is the despair that withholds assurance from ordinary saints as if it were a privileged possession reserved for the unusually mature, the unusually pious, or those who have passed through some specific spiritual experience the rest have not. The Reformed tradition’s sustained insistence has been that plērophoria is the privilege of every believer—the normal Christian standing, addressed by the apostles to ordinary saints in their ordinary letters—and that the absence of assurance is a problem to be remedied rather than a humility to be embraced. The Westminster Confession (18.3): this infallible assurance doth not so belong to the essence of faith, but that a true believer may wait long, and conflict with many difficulties, before he be partaker of it: yet, being enabled by the Spirit to know the things which are freely given him of God, he may, without extraordinary revelation, in the right use of ordinary means, attain thereunto. Recover both ends. Refuse the presumption that claims assurance apart from the marks of regenerate life, and refuse the despair that withholds it from ordinary saints. The biblical plērophoria is the Spirit-wrought settled conviction of what God has given, grounded in the objective gospel and confirmed by the Spirit’s witness to the marks of regenerate life—the rest in the Father’s love that the apostles uniformly assume their hearers can know.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek plērophoria (full assurance, full conviction) from plēro- (full) + phor- (to bear): the soul borne fully into settled conviction. Four NT uses (Col 2:2; 1 Thess 1:5; Heb 6:11; 10:22), structurally clustering into assurance of understanding, hope, and faith; the privilege of every believer through the Spirit’s witness to the Word.

expand to see more

Greek plērophoria (G4136) — full assurance, full conviction (Col 2:2; 1 Thess 1:5; Heb 6:11; 10:22).

Greek plērophoreō (G4135) — to bring in full measure, fully persuade, fully accomplish (Luke 1:1; Rom 4:21; 14:5; Col 4:12; 2 Tim 4:5, 17).

Greek plērēs (G4134) — full (the adjective).

Greek pherō (G5342) — to bear, carry (the second element of the compound).

Usage

"Full assurance of understanding... full assurance of hope... full assurance of faith—the three clustered apostolic uses (Col 2:2; Heb 6:11; Heb 10:22) name a structural doctrine."

"Plērophoria is the privilege of every believer through the Spirit’s witness to the Word, not a privileged possession of the few."

"Presumption claims assurance apart from regenerate marks; despair withholds it from ordinary saints; biblical pattern grounds assurance in the gospel and confirms it by the Spirit’s witness to the marks of new life."
